title: A Better Priest, a New Agreement
overview: The writer argues that Jesus serves as priest in heaven itself and brings the new agreement between God and people that the prophet Jeremiah had promised.

parts.label: The priest seated in heaven (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: The writer sums up the argument so far: Jesus is the great high priest, now seated in the place of honor beside God's throne. He serves in the true place of worship that God set up, of which the old sacred tent was only a picture.

parts.label: What a priest must offer (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: Priests under the law of Moses came from one family line and presented offerings, so Jesus could not serve as that kind of priest on earth; later chapters say what he offered was himself. The tent Moses built followed a pattern God showed him on the mountain, so the writer treats it as a copy and shadow of something heavenly.

parts.label: A better agreement (v. 6)
parts.note: A covenant is a binding agreement between God and a people, and Jesus is pictured as the go-between who brings a new one. The writer says it rests on better promises, which he spells out in the quotation that follows.

parts.label: Why a new agreement was needed (vv. 7-9)
parts.note: The writer quotes Jeremiah, a prophet from around the time Babylon conquered Jerusalem, who foresaw a new covenant with Israel and Judah. The fault named is that the people did not keep the agreement God made when he led them out of Egypt, not that God's law itself was bad.

parts.label: What the new agreement promises (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: God promises to put his laws in people's minds and write them on their hearts, so that everyone, from least to greatest, knows him personally, and to forgive their wrongs and remember them no more. Jeremiah first spoke this to Israel and Judah, and Christians read it as fulfilled through Jesus.

parts.label: The old one fading away (v. 13)
parts.note: By calling the agreement new, the writer reasons, God marked the first one as old and soon to disappear. Many scholars think this was written while the Jerusalem temple and its sacrifices still stood, before the Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

disagreement: Christians genuinely differ on what calling the first covenant obsolete means for God's ongoing relationship with the Jewish people, with some seeing it as replaced and others seeing God's promises to Israel as still standing.
think: What difference might it make whether the way you live comes from rules handed to you or from something written on your heart?
